gap: The gap named last round is CLOSED and I proved it on the real product: the replace-based bounce adds nothing to the Back stack. Four chip clicks made while already on the History page held window.history.length flat at 23 -> 23 -> 23 -> 23 -> 23 while the selection moved row 1 -> 6 -> 15 -> 29 -> 6 and the address matched the screen every time. What is still open is the SAME defect on the other leg of the same function, the first-use leg, which nobody has looked at and which no round has touched since round 7. showRestoreVersion (tv-break-dashboard/src/kai/assistant-panel-state.js:107) calls writeAddress(pointAddress(versionId)) FIRST, and writeAddress is a replaceState on the entry the operator is currently standing on, so the ?entry=version:<id> address is stamped onto the page being LEFT; only then does window.location.hash = 'Versions' push the new entry. Measured on port 8087 from the Today page with the dock open: one chip click pushed exactly one entry (history.length 23 -> 24, correct) and landed on the History page at ?p9c=r4b&entry=version:a770ecb90600#Versions with the right row selected, and then ONE Back press landed the operator on the Today page at http://127.0.0.1:8087/?p9c=r4b&entry=version%3Aa770ecb90600, hash empty, main heading 'היום, רשת 13' (screenshot p9-c4-01-back-from-first-use-lands-on-overview-with-version-address.png). That is exactly the address-bar-says-one-thing, screen-shows-another failure the last three rounds existed to end, and it is one click plus the most ordinary browser gesture there is. Copy that link and your colleague opens Today. It is NOT a regression this round caused (the first-use leg is byte-identical to HEAD), which is why it survived: both prior rounds fixed the repeat-use leg and left this one alone. THE FIX, one pass inside P9's own file, no P8 file touched, and I ran it myself in the live page: stop calling writeAddress on the page you are leaving and push the whole destination address in a single navigation instead. Build the target from the CURRENT search so no other query param is lost (new URLSearchParams(window.location.search), set ADDRESS_PARAM to pointAddress(versionId), keep the rest), then window.history.pushState(null, '', pathname + '?' + params + '#Versions') and window.dispatchEvent(new HashChangeEvent('hashchange')). Measured live: history.length 27 -> 28 (exactly one entry), HistoryPage mounted and selected the addressed row (the 37 restore point), the Overview heading NEVER painted (a 4 ms poll across the whole transition saw only 'היסטוריה'), and one Back press landed on the clean http://127.0.0.1:8087/?p9c=r4d with no entry param at all. Leave the already-on-Versions leg exactly as it shipped: I tested replaceState plus a synthetic hashchange there and it does NOT remount (the hash does not change, so the shell keeps the same view and the row stayed on the previous selection), which is precisely why the bounce exists. Pin it in tests/test_p9_kai_history_second_use.py, whose CDP harness already drives a real browser: after the first use, assert history.length rose by exactly one AND that history.back() returns to an entry whose search carries no ADDRESS_PARAM. The pre-fix control for this one is the shipped first-use leg itself, which returns to an entry that DOES carry it.

No Linear or agent tool is exposed to this session (ToolSearch for a Linear agent returns Azure SRE, SendMessage and WebFetch, nothing product-like), and the two signed-in Linear tabs in the shared browser belong to other builders mid-task, which I will not drive. What I did run myself, and label as documentation rather than a live comparison: I fetched Figma's published version-history article directly. It documents that a version is previewed by selecting it in the sidebar and seeing it in the viewport, that a restore is non-destructive because two checkpoints are written, and that a single version is addressable through the row menu's Copy link. Kai matches all three in substance and beats the documented model on one point, because Kai shows the field-level before and after of the undo (revenue_weight 39 -> 35, on kairos_settings.json) before you commit to it, which Figma's docs do not describe. Where Kai still falls short is exactly the mechanic these rounds keep circling: Figma's version opens in place, while Kai's repeat click tears the workspace down through the Today page and back, and Kai's first click leaves the version address stamped on the page you came from.
